Policy iteration

Lesson 30 finds a policy's values. Lesson 31 turns values into a better policy. Alternate the two and the policy keeps improving until it stops changing, at which point it is optimal.

The bridge. Reach the goal (+10) without falling into the water (−10). Every other move gives $0$, and $\gamma = 0.9$. The ice is slippery: you move the way you meant with probability $1 - \text{slip}$, otherwise sideways, half each way. Walls and edges leave you in place. Click a cell to turn its arrow.

roundevaluation sweepsarrows changed$v_\pi(\text{S})$

Each evaluation runs Lesson 30's in-place sweeps until $\Delta < 10^{-4}$. Amber outlines mark arrows the last improvement changed. Try slip 0, 0.1 and 0.3. At 0 the best route crosses the bridge. At 0.1 it takes the top detour. At 0.3 most bridge cells point into the wall above, so a slip can only go sideways along the bridge, never into the water.

The maths

Policy iteration alternates evaluation (E) and greedy improvement (I), starting from any policy $\pi_0$:

$$\pi_0 \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_{\pi_0} \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_1 \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_{\pi_1} \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_2 \xrightarrow{\;E\;} \cdots \xrightarrow{\;I\;} \pi_* \xrightarrow{\;E\;} v_*$$

Each arrow is one button. Evaluation solves for $v_{\pi_i}$. Improvement sets

$$\pi_{i+1}(s) = \arg\max_a \sum_{s', r} p(s', r \mid s, a)\,\big[r + \gamma\, v_{\pi_i}(s')\big]$$

keeping the old action when it is already among the best.

Why it stops. By the policy improvement theorem (Lesson 31), $v_{\pi_{i+1}} \ge v_{\pi_i}$ in every state, and if the policy changes, some state strictly improves. So no policy can come back once it has been left. A finite MDP has finitely many deterministic policies, $|\mathcal{A}|^{|\mathcal{S}|}$ of them, so the sequence must end. It ends when improvement changes nothing, which by Lesson 31 means the policy is optimal.

Why keep the old action on ties. If two actions are equally good and improvement switched between them freely, the policy could flip back and forth forever without getting better (S&B Exercise 4.4). Changing only on a strict improvement rules that out.

In practice policy iteration takes very few rounds compared with $|\mathcal{A}|^{|\mathcal{S}|}$. Here there are $4^{21}$ deterministic policies and it needs fewer than ten rounds. The cost sits inside each evaluation, which is a full loop of sweeps on its own.
